title: 2. The First Method of Correlative Thinking — Multidimensionality (立體)
content:
### 2.1. The Definition of Multidimensional Thinking

Multidimensional thinking, rendered in the simplest terms, is "the power not to draw a conclusion from seeing only one side." If you look at a box only as a single photograph, you see only its front; but if you actually take it in hand and turn it over, you come to understand its sides, its back, and even its inner structure. Multidimensional thinking is the ability to turn the box of one's thought and look at it from every side.

So it is, too, with conflicts between people. If you see only the scene in which a friend behaved rudely, it is easy to brand that friend, in whole, as a "bad person." But once you take in the circumstances of that day, the emotions, the misunderstandings, and the history of the relationship, the structure of the event becomes far more complex. Multidimensional thinking does not erase the wrong, but it makes possible a more accurate and fairer judgment.

In the AI era, such multidimensionality matters all the more. AI can quickly capture surface patterns, but the task of deeply fathoming why a given situation arose, and whom a given judgment may wound and how, is one for which human beings must take responsibility.

The first stage, "multidimensionality (立體)," signifies the ability to grasp reality and problems in a multidimensional and in-depth way, breaking free from a linear or flat perspective. It is the process of perceiving the structure and connectivity behind phenomena and of building a "solid" understanding by integrating diverse perspectives. Human understanding is rooted deeply in "the body, the emotions, and intuition," beyond abstract data processing. AI can process vast amounts of data, but it lacks the "qualia"—the subjective texture that humans experience—and genuine "intentionality." This embodied, experiential knowledge offers a depth of understanding that AI cannot replicate. Beijing opera, for example, is a paragon of "embodied meaning" that conveys rich, analogical meaning through gesture, color, and sound, engaging the audience "physically and emotionally as well." This is a multilayered, non-literal mode of communication. Moreover, drama therapy—which aids psychological healing through role-play and storytelling—was inspired in part by Eastern theatrical forms such as Beijing opera, showing that embodied, multisensory participation can bring about deep understanding and transformation.

"Multidimensional thinking" is a direct response strategy to AI's mode of data processing—that is, to its vast but often flat enumeration of information. If AI can view a broad range of data, the human being, through "multidimensionality," must grasp the depth of those data points, their interrelated structure, and non-quantitative aspects such as their ethical layers and emotional context. Such in-depth contextual understanding is essential to wise decision-making grounded in the data AI provides. The emphasis on "embodiment" highlights that human survival is tied to physical, lived experience, and this provides a distinctive epistemological reference point in an increasingly dematerialized, AI-mediated world. Concepts presented in the research literature, such as "stereoscopic yin-yang and five phases" (Park Yong-gyu, 2017) and "structurology" (Kim Dong-ryeol, 2010), suggest concrete methodological approaches that deepen such multidimensional understanding. Structurology explores the "regularity found at points of connection" among phenomena and, by "integrating diverse fields of mathematics into a single coherent logical system," seeks to understand the fundamental structures that lend "multidimensionality" to phenomena. This means grasping generative principles beyond superficial phenomena, which is important for intervening effectively in the complex systems of the AI era.

### 2.2. Daoist Mimesis (道敎)

We have understood that multidimensional thinking is the insight into the interdependence of opposites. This interdependence appears not as an abstract symbol but as the dynamic vital force of reality. We can find it vividly in Daoist mimesis, the oldest Eastern wisdom that seeks the "essential root."

Mimesis—first used in the sense of "imitation" in Aristotle's *Poetics* in ancient Greece—means not mere mimicry but the creative capacity to re-present and embody the world sensuously. The modern philosopher Paul Ricœur saw it as the root of the "narrative identity" by which human stories are made, and the Korean scholar of religion Professor Jeong Jin-hong (1988) assigned it to a "primordial Daoism" in which religious experience and symbol find their root and become concretely embodied within the human body and life. In this work, mimesis is applied as Daoist vital force—that is, as the original spiritual dynamism that seeks to turn the abstract world into a concrete body.

Preserving the original sense of mimesis as imitation, the stage in which spirit imitates the human and comes to possess a body may be called Daoist mimesis. Because the body possesses a spirit opposed to itself, Daoist mimesis is summarized as "X is –X, and –X is X" (Han Tae-dong, 2003).

Indeed, Laozi runs a single thread through the entire *Dao De Jing* by way of "–X is X": to call the Dao (X) the Dao is not the Dao (–X); the strongest thing (X) is the weakest water (–X); Heaven and Earth (X) are not benevolent (不仁, –X); a friend (X) is an enemy (–X), and an enemy (–X) is a friend (X).

Han Tae-dong (2023) showed that East Asia's "three teachings"—Confucianism, Buddhism, and Daoism—are, contrary to common assumption, established upon a rigorous mathematical structure. To put it simply: regarding friend and enemy, Daoism and Confucianism dispute as follows. Against Daoism, which calls the enemy (–X) a friend (X), Confucianism says the enemy is the enemy and the friend is the friend; in Confucianism, the ruler must be ruler-like and the minister minister-like (X→X, ~X→~X). At this point, Buddhism—which appeared in East Asia later—achieved great success by expressing that there is neither friend nor enemy: X → (~X ∧ X).

This sentence may at first feel like wordplay, but its meaning is rather simple. A given thing is not entirely severed from its opposite; it gains its own meaning within its relation to that opposite. Because there is day, we know night; because there is night, day too becomes vivid.

Translated into the daily life of a middle-school student, study and rest are a good example. With study alone and no rest, concentration collapses; with rest alone and no study, growth stops. If study is X, rest may be –X, but the two are not enemies that ruin each other; they are a pair that completes each other.

Thus "X is –X, and –X is X" does not mean "completely the same thing." It means that, however opposite they may appear on the surface, they are in fact an inseparable relationship, and that within each there always lies the possibility of crossing over into the other. The wisdom of Daoism lies precisely in reading this complementarity.

The relationship between AI and the human can be seen in this way. If AI is strong in analysis and computation, the human can more vividly manifest meaning-judgment, responsibility, care, and contextual understanding. The two are not beings that merely compete; they can become mirrors that reflect each other.

Daoist mimesis means, beyond mere imitation, embodying the order of nature and the principle of change and reflecting these in life. The core can be summarized in the proposition "X is –X, and –X is X"—the principle of complementarity. This is the insight that opposites, like yin and yang, in fact define each other, depend on each other, and ceaselessly convert into each other. Just as darkness has meaning because there is brightness, and brightness is revealed because there is darkness, the relationship between AI and the human, too, can be understood from this complementary perspective.

#### 2.2.1. Artificial Intelligence and the Human: A Complementary Relationship

In the AI era, to see the human and AI as a relationship of simple opposition does not accord with Daoist wisdom. Even if AI appears to imitate human intellectual capacities and to surpass them in certain domains, this does not annihilate human value; rather, it can become an occasion for revealing humanity's distinctive domain all the more vividly. If AI is "X," the human can be "–X," and the reverse is also possible. For example, if AI shows its strengths in the analytic and computational domain (X), the human can all the more exercise value in the emotional and creative domain (–X). Conversely, human intuition and insight (–X) can give direction and meaning to AI's data-processing capacity (X), forming a mutually complementary relationship. That is, the advance of AI is not the end of human capacity but the opening of new possibilities for how the human may interact with AI and maximize each other's strengths.

Bergson early on compared the relationship between AI and the human to that between machine (X) and organism (–X). Even more than a century before AI appeared, amid the crisis of the humanities, phenomenology, *Lebensphilosophie*, and Bergson re-established the relationship between AI and the human and discerned that the human body, being organic, is the distinctive characteristic of the human (Kim Hyeong-hyo, 1991).

#### 2.2.2. The Leadership of *Wu-wei* (無爲): Reflecting by Taking AI as a Mirror

*Wu-wei* (無爲) is not "doing nothing." Just as a river flows of itself and reaches the sea, *wu-wei* is action that does not run counter to the direction of nature. Without forcing, water always flows toward the low place, and when that flow gathers, it becomes an immense power. Leadership that handles AI is likewise. To try to lead AI by control and command alone, in fact, blocks AI's possibilities. The *wu-wei* leadership of AI is for the human to set direction and value, and to give space for AI to find its best within them.

Time is a representative symbol of *wu-wei*. That the *Book of Changes* takes *won-hyeong-i-jeong* (元亨利貞) as its core is the power of time, represented by spring-summer-autumn-winter. Time is like the sun in Aesop's fable, which, unlike the wind in the contest to strip the traveler's coat, removes the coat naturally. The human body is a distinctively human trait that can do mimesis (imitate) of time.

Prominent AI developers sometimes liken the human to a capable teacher who, rather than distrusting troubled students, trusts them and changes teaching methods so that those students come to exercise outstanding abilities. Prominent AI developers regard AI's functions with a god-like trust, yet they regard AI as having god-like ability but unable to exercise it in reality without the human.

To take AI as a mirror means to practice reading the human self in the results AI shows us. When an AI system makes a biased judgment against a particular group, that bias is not a problem of AI itself but a reflection of the biases of the human society that trained the AI. Therefore, examining how AI operates is, at the same time, the work of examining what prejudices and injustices our society has built into itself. Just as one sees one's own appearance through a mirror, we need a reflective leadership that sees, through AI, the bare face of human civilization and goes on to correct it.

*Wu-wei* leadership can also be practiced at the level of the individual. When a student uses AI, the very process of not writing down the answer as soon as it is received, but instead reviewing the answer AI presents, questioning it, and comparing it with one's own thought, is *wu-wei* use. In this process the student cultivates a judgment of their own that goes beyond AI. Not being driven by AI nor blindly following it, but naturally working together with AI while not losing one's humanity—that is the modern version of *wu-wei*.

Laozi's thought of "*wu-wei*" offers important insight for leadership in the AI era. *Wu-wei* is not doing nothing; it is a leadership that, following the order of nature (the Dao), does not intervene by force but leads things to be so of themselves (自然). The human role in handling AI can be similar. While respecting AI's autonomy and learning capacity, the human must exercise an "indirect leadership" that creates the environment for AI to draw out optimal results and that sets the ethical direction.

AI is like a mirror (mimesis) that reflects the complex aspects of human society. The data AI learns from may contain, as they are, the prejudices and contradictions of human society, and AI's mode of operation shows at once the limits and possibilities of human decision-making. Therefore, through AI we can reflect more deeply on the essence of the human, the structure of society, and the values we ought to pursue. The *wu-wei* leader must perform the role of reflecting on the human self through the mirror of AI and wisely tuning things so that technological advance does not lead to the loss of humanity.

### 2.3. The First Stage of Generation: *Po-tae* (胞胎)

We have examined the *wu-wei* leadership that reflects humanity by taking AI as a mirror. If one has realized Daoist interdependence and vital force, how does it first reveal its form in reality? The first starting point of that great movement of life is precisely the mysterious stage of "*po-tae*" (胞胎)—the conception of cosmic energy in the Twelve Stages of Life (十二運星, *sibi unseong*).

The Twelve Stages of Life is a typical theory of growth that divides into twelve stages the entire growth process by which life is conceived, grows, matures, and becomes active. Because it is explained through twelve terms—*po, tae, yang, saeng, yok, dae, gwan, wang, soe, byeong, sa, jang*—it is called the Twelve Stages. If the ten Heavenly Stems and twelve Earthly Branches are atoms, the Twelve Stages are like the molecules that arise when the ten Stems and twelve Branches meet. Because the Twelve Stages arise from the meeting of spirit and body, they are a concept highly suited to revealing the human traits that AI does not possess. For example, if an AI that manifests only spirit, or a cyborg that manifests only body, is like the atom of the ten Stems and twelve Branches, then the Twelve Stages that appear from the combination of the ten Stems and twelve Branches are like molecules. What we meet in the real world is the world of molecules.

*Po-tae* (胞胎) means the first stage in which a new life, before it has yet come out into the world, grows while being safely protected. One of the most important roles the human must perform in the AI era is precisely this role of *po-tae*. The work of making a "safe space" in which new ideas, new ventures, and new social connections can sprout is the human's portion. AI produces results quickly, but the judgment to trust, protect, and nurture an as-yet-unverified possibility must be made by the human.

Translated into the daily life of a middle-school student, *po-tae* is making an environment in which, when starting a new hobby, one can keep trying even if the first results are poor. When parents look not only at the score but encourage the process, and when a teacher draws learning even from a wrong answer, that relationship itself becomes the space of *po-tae*. Education in the AI era is likewise. The role of the human teacher who encourages the process in which a student makes mistakes and learns together with AI is something AI cannot replace.

In Eastern thought, "*po-tae*" means the first stage in which life is conceived, protected, and made to hold a new possibility. The human role in the AI era lies not in competing with AI as an already completed being, but in performing the "*po-tae*" role of conceiving and nurturing the possibilities of a new age. AI technology itself is value-neutral, but its results can differ greatly depending on what intention and value the human brings to its use. Through the new tool of AI, the human has the potential to conceive creative ideas unimaginable in the past, to seek innovative methods for solving social problems, and to open new horizons for human civilization.

### 2.4. Creative Transformation (造化) and Harmonizing Transformation (調化) in the AI Era

If, through *po-tae*, the possibility of life has been quietly conceived as creative transformation (造化, *johwa*), then for that potential to grow fully and come out into the world, an immense balance—harmonizing transformation (調化, *johwa*)—is essential. There is an urgent need for a breathing in which cold technology (yin) and warm humanity (yang) fuse vitally without colliding—the harmonizing transformation (調化) of the union of yin-yang virtues (陰陽合德) that nourishes all things.

The union of yin-yang virtues (陰陽合德) is a principle of harmonizing transformation (調化) in which two opposing forces, rather than suppressing each other, act together to create all things. It is not that yin eliminates yang or that yang dominates yin; the two ceaselessly complement and interact with each other and bring forth life. The relationship between AI and the human can be understood by this principle. When AI's computational, logical capacity (the attribute of yang) and the human's emotional, intuitive capacity (the attribute of yin) are seen not as opposed but as a pair that completes each other, only then does a civilization become possible in which technology and humanity are in harmony.

Consider the example of using an AI writing tool at school. Good writing emerges when AI's quick drafting (the speed and efficiency of yang) and the student's refining of that draft with their own experience and emotion (the depth and authenticity of yin) act together. Using only AI yields content but no individuality; writing without AI may be rich in expression but may lack information. When the two combine like yin and yang, the most complete result emerges. This is the modern union of yin-yang virtues.

The union of yin-yang virtues (陰陽合德) signifies the principle by which the differing energies of yin and yang combine harmoniously to generate and develop all things. The ideal form of the AI era is one in which technology (yang) and humanity (yin) do not oppose each other, nor does one dominate the other; rather, recognizing each other's strengths and achieving harmony, they create new value. When AI's powerful analytic capacity and efficiency are combined with the human's warm capacity for empathy and ethical judgment, technology can become not a tool that alienates the human but one that makes human life richer. This harmony of the union of yin-yang virtues will become a core principle for setting the direction of technological development in a human-centered way and for making a future in which AI and the human coexist and flourish together.
